SM18A-A1.free_elimination: none: all four options satisfy m<=36 (real t-roots) and m>0; nothing struck without solving
SM18A-A1.on_blueprint: borderline-yes: polynomial equation in one variable solved by factoring/quadratic form, inside Nonlinear equations in one variable; t=x^2 is a device, not a separate construct. Accept, but it is at the edge of what the Digital SAT prints.
SM18A-A1.note: Decision point is real (two x per positive t, so exactly two x means a repeated positive t). Desmos bypass is total: graph y=x^4-12x^2, read the minimum -36. Back-substitution also works. Key is the largest option; 36=(12/2)^2 echoes the printed 12.

SM18A-A2.free_elimination: option (a) has no exponent while the stem says growth is exponential: struck structurally. Evaluated: (a) 3103.33, (b) 3194.40, (c) 3221.02, (d) 3375.18; true value 2000*1.331^(5/3)=3221.02 = (c) only.
SM18A-A2.on_blueprint: yes: exponential growth, per-interval rate to per-unit factor (nonlinear functions)
SM18A-A2.note: Recognising 1.331=1.1^3 is a genuine decision point and (d) is the trap a rate-divider falls into. Bypass: a calculator evaluates 1.331^(5/3) and each option in under a minute. Options are ascending by value; key third. Good item.

SM18A-A3.note: Two remainder conditions then a 2x2 linear system and one evaluation: a grind, not a decision point. The only twist is that 2x+2 gives p(-1) with the remainder unchanged, which is a fact, not an insight; distractor -17 (halving) is plausible but a student who just plugs x=-1 never meets it. Author says hard; the real hard route uses one remainder plus a structural trick. Key is the smallest option.

SM18A-A4.free_elimination: none formally; but 11 = 5(4)-9, the numerator at the excluded value, so a student who sees that the fractions must match at x=4 gets it in one step (that is the solve, not a leak)
SM18A-A4.on_blueprint: yes: rational equation with a parameter, no-solution case
SM18A-A4.note: Standard SAT no-solution rational item: clear denominators, solve, check the excluded value. One step, well-drilled. DUPLICATE SKILL with B4, which contains this exact move plus a second case; keep one. Key third; two negatives, no sole-odd-one-out.

SM18A-A5.free_elimination: -16 falls with no arithmetic: radius is sqrt(50) about 7, and a circle centred at x=-16 cannot reach the y-axis. The stem's rejection step IS a free elimination, so the 'other tangency value' distractor is inert. Rejection verified: |a+6|/sqrt2 = sqrt50 for a=4 and a=-16; a=-16 spans x in [-23.07,-8.93], misses the y-axis.
SM18A-A5.on_blueprint: borderline: circle-line tangency via discriminant is a nonlinear system (Advanced Math) but the circle equation and the distance-to-line route belong to Geometry and Trig; the Digital SAT does print 'intersect at exactly one point' items, so accept with the domain caveat
SM18A-A5.note: After the free strike it is a routine distance-from-centre-to-line computation with one candidate that fits. Desmos slider on a settles it instantly. Key is the largest option and the LARGER of the two candidates (see B3: same pattern).

SM18A-A6.free_elimination: none by mathematics. PARITY TELL: 18 is the sole even option among 13, 25, 27.
SM18A-A6.note: Solved: u=sqrt(2x+14); u=0 gives x=-7 (checks 0=0); x-1=3u gives x=25 (24*8=192 ok) and x=-5 extraneous (-12 vs 12). Sum 18. Good algebra item with two genuine decision points (do not divide by the radical; check extraneous). Desmos bypass: graph both sides, read intersections -7 and 25. Distractors are 'sum of a wrong subset' (13 = all three roots, 25 = one root) - a recipe shared with B6's option 4. Fix the option parity before insertion.

SM18A-A7.free_elimination: 63 falls with one mental average: f is increasing, g(4)=7 is below the midpoint of 1 and 14, so f(g(4)) is below (15+93)/2=54. Cheap but not zero arithmetic; counted as 1.
SM18A-A7.on_blueprint: yes: function composition with a table, linear function from two points
SM18A-A7.note: Read two table rows, fit a line through two points, evaluate. No decision point; a standard medium composition item. Author says hard: disagree. Key third.

SM18A-B1.free_elimination: 1 and 2.5 fall with no arithmetic: the ledge (480) is below the launch height (576), so the projectile reaches it only on the way down, after it returns to 576 ft at t=2*2.5=5. Also 2.5 is the vertex time, at which it is at its maximum, not at 480. Remaining: 6 vs 9.
SM18A-B1.note: h(1)=640, h(2.5)=676, h(6)=480, h(9)=0. Four evaluations of h settle it; the negative root can never be an option so the 'rejection' is not a decision point. Standard medium item. DROP from a hard batch. 'Vertex coordinate offered as a distractor' recipe shared with B6 (option 4).

SM18A-B2.free_elimination: none by mathematics; the two decimal options (6.8, 8.5) read as manufactured distractors on an integer-exponent item, but that is test-wisdom not a strike
SM18A-B2.note: Rewrite as powers of 2: 3x-3=-2x+62, x=13. The bases 8 and 1/4 are both obviously powers of 2; the SAT prints this at medium. Back-substitution or Desmos trivial. Key is the largest option. Author says hard: disagree.

SM18A-B3.free_elimination: 7 falls with no arithmetic: both roots negative means the sum -(k-15)/3 < 0, so k>15 (Vieta sign read, which is the stem's own rejection step). Then k=23 and k=25 give discriminants -368 and -380: NO REAL ROOTS, violating the stem's premise that there are two real solutions. A student who checks the three remaining options for real roots reaches 55 without ever using the one-is-triple-the-other condition. Rejection verified: k=7 gives roots 2/3 and 2 (positive); k=55 gives -10/3 and -10.
SM18A-B3.on_blueprint: yes: sum and product of roots with a parameter
SM18A-B3.note: As authored the Vieta route is genuinely hard (m^2-32m-320=0, m=40 or -8), but the distractor set defeats it: two of three distractors fail the stem's premise, the third is a free sign strike. DROP or re-author distractors so that every option gives two real negative roots (need k>15 and (k-15)^2 >= 12(2k-10), e.g. k=45, 63). Same 'other root of the parameter quadratic is the distractor, and the key is the larger candidate' recipe as A5.

SM18A-B4.free_elimination: none; k=12 (coefficient match) is easy to find but the partner is not readable from the options (17-12=5, 19-12=7, 31-12=19, 60-12=48 all look plausible)
SM18A-B4.on_blueprint: yes: rational equation with a parameter, no-solution cases
SM18A-B4.note: Two distinct no-solution mechanisms (0=-21 identity failure; candidate equals excluded value) must both be found and summed. Verified: k=12 gives 0=-21; k=5 gives x=3, excluded. Desmos slider does not display 'no solution' cleanly, so the algebra is needed. Best item in the batch. Supersedes A4 (contains its whole move). Key is the smallest option.

SM18A-B5.free_elimination: none: all options negative (f(1) is negative since f(0)=-6 and no zero lies in (0,1)); no magnitude bound without computing
SM18A-B5.on_blueprint: yes: polynomial zeros and multiplicity from graph behaviour
SM18A-B5.note: a=-6/18=-1/3, f(1)=(-1/3)(4)(3)(2)=-8. The multiplicity-2 decision is required and not Desmos-able (no function given). Distractors are the three natural errors. Key is the largest option (least negative).

SM18A-B6.free_elimination: none strictly, but structural necessity collapses the item: any solution set of |p(x)|=k is symmetric about the axis x=4, so three solutions sum to 3*4=12 with no reference to k=49. A student who knows this never finds k at all.
SM18A-B6.on_blueprint: borderline-yes: absolute value of a quadratic with a solution-count condition; SAT prints |linear|=k counts and quadratic-vertex items, this fuses them. Accept.
SM18A-B6.note: Verified: k=49 at vertex x=4; other two solutions 4 +/- sqrt98 sum to 8; total 12. Intended path (find k at the reflected vertex) is hard; the symmetry shortcut makes it a one-liner for a strong student, which is legitimate SAT behaviour rather than a leak. Desmos bypass: slider on k, read three intersections. Distractor 4 is the 'vertex coordinate offered as the answer' recipe (shared with B1's 2.5); 49 is the intermediate k. Key second-smallest.

SM18A-B7.free_elimination: denominator closure: half-spacing is 2.5, so the vertex depth 3*(2.5)^2 must have fractional part .75 (or c=3*0.5*5.5 has .25) - a student who sees the 5/2 knows the answer has denominator 4 and strikes -27 and -7.5. Cheap, but it requires the setup, so I count it as 1 (the -7.5 option, which is 3*2.5 with no square, is also struck as dimensionally wrong).
SM18A-B7.on_blueprint: yes: equivalent forms of a quadratic, vertex from intercept spacing
SM18A-B7.note: Axis x=3, intercepts 0.5 and 5.5, g(3)=3(2.5)(-2.5)=-18.75; c=8.25 checks. The spacing-to-depth relation is a real decision point; the grind route (36-4c/3=25) also gets there, so bypassable by routine algebra. Key third; sole integer option (-27) is not the key.
